turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I've put Dr Naidoo's script on the desk. It says amoxicillin five hundred milligrams three times a day, started Monday, for sinusitis.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not what I've got. The bottle says two hundred and fifty milligrams, and I take that three times a day. I checked before we left, so I don't know where five hundred comes from.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box in our cupboard says five hundred, love. I saw it last night. Maybe there are two strengths floating around.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): The dose on the script and the dose you're describing don't match, so I won't guess a number. We'll come back to it. What's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): This rash. It itches like mad and I can't think. It might be something I ate, or the new cream, or the antibiotic, and I'm really frightened it's going to get worse.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll take those apart. When did the rash and the itch actually start?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, Thursday night, or Friday morning, I honestly can't say which. A few days, that's as close as I can get.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it going to spread to my face? Will it leave scars? Should I have gone to casualty instead?
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Reasonable things to worry about. I don't want to reassure you until I've looked. Where is it sitting worst?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): On my arms and my tummy, and across the chest. Red bumps that itch, some of them joining up. Well, actually a few on my neck as well. Not on the face.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the lips or tongue? Any chest tightness or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, and my breathing is normal. I'm sure about that part.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever, or feeling properly drained?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt hot yesterday afternoon, but I didn't check it, and I don't feel hot today. I am tired, and I'm sleeping badly from the itch. Is the tiredness a bad sign?
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Obs before she came in: temperature thirty six point eight, pulse eighty two, blood pressure one thirty two over eighty four, sats ninety eight percent.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok, I won't argue with the cuff. Can those numbers still be normal if this is an allergy? That's what I'm scared of.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): They can. Normal blood pressure and oxygen just mean you're stable in the chair. They don't name the rash. Talk me through the antibiotic, the cream, and what you ate.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Monday the GP started amoxicillin tablets for sinusitis, three times a day, whatever the strength is. Tuesday I opened a new Epimax cream from the chemist, twice a day on my arms and legs, for dry skin. Wednesday there were prawns at my brother's braai. All three happened, and I can't tell you which one did this.

[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This is the same thing she had with penicillin as a child. Her mother told me she came out in blotches and they called it an allergy. Nobody seems to have written it down.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not true. I am not allergic to penicillin. I took it years ago and I was fine. She's mixing me up with my brother, so please don't record an allergy I don't have.

[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to collapse those two accounts into one. I'll record that your husband remembers a childhood penicillin rash and that you deny it. It matters, because amoxicillin is a penicillin. Thinking it through, this could be the drug, the cream, or the prawns, and I can't separate them yet.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it the antibiotic then? Do I stop it today? What happens to the sinus if I stop? And do I throw the cream out?

[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not choosing one. A drug eruption, contact dermatitis from the Epimax, and a food reaction are all still open. Nothing is confirmed. Prawns usually give hives that shift around, and a fixed bumpy rash sits a bit less well with that, so food is lower on the list, not off it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mine doesn't move, it just stays and itches. So food is unlikely? Sorry, I know I keep asking.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Less likely, not impossible. Let me look.

[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): There's a widespread red papular rash on both arms, the abdomen and the upper chest, plus a few lesions on the neck. No swelling of the lips. No wheeze while you talk. The skin over the rash is warm, not clammy.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Warm, so is it infected? Do I need a different antibiotic? That feels mad if an antibiotic started it.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Warmth over a rash is not cellulitis. I don't see pus, and there's no spreading hot edge. I wouldn't add another antibiotic today.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): How long does a rash like this take to fade if I stop everything? And is Epimax even known for this? The pharmacist said it was gentle, so I thought it was safe.

[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Epimax is bland for most people, which is why it's used on dry skin, but a new product can still irritate or occasionally sensitise. A drug rash often appears a few days after the first tablet, so Monday to Thursday fits, and Tuesday for the cream fits as well. The timing doesn't pick a winner. That's where I am.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what is the actual plan? I can't leave with three maybes and no instruction.

[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stop the amoxicillin from today, and stop the Epimax as well, until this is clearer. If the sinus aches, paracetamol is fine, not a new antibiotic. For the itch I'll prescribe cetirizine ten milligrams by mouth, once a day, at night.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams at night. Will it knock me out? Can I drive to work in the morning? What if the itch doesn't budge?

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): It makes some people drowsy, so take it at night and see how you feel before you drive. A cool cloth will do more than scratching. If it barely helps we can talk again, but start with that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): And the prawns, do I avoid all seafood for life? There's another braai this weekend and my brother will dish up.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Avoid prawns and other shellfish for now, not forever. Ordinary food is fine. We'll revisit it when I see you again.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can you test her for penicillin today, so this argument is over?

[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not today. We might arrange patch testing if the rash has not settled in two weeks. I'm not booking it now. Bloods or a scan wouldn't answer this, so those aren't on the cards.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Does patch testing hurt? Is it on the back? If I skip it, could we miss something dangerous?

[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Small discs taped to the back, left on for a couple of days, more itchy than painful. We only consider it if you're not better. The danger signs are lip or tongue swelling, wheezing, or blisters with you feeling very unwell. If any of those happen, go to casualty and don't wait for the appointment.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Swelling, wheeze, blisters, casualty. I'm putting that in my phone. Do I come back even if it fades?
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Let's see you in two weeks either way. If it hasn't settled by then, that's when we might do the patch test. Reception will book the visit.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): What if the sinus blows up before two weeks? And can I work? I just sit at a desk.

[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Work is fine. If the sinus pain or a fever comes back hard, or the rash spreads quickly, phone sooner. Otherwise two weeks stands. I'm not putting a firm diagnosis on this today.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll watch her at home. The dog will be glad we're back, she's been whining at the gate. We must fetch the cetirizine from the chemist, hey?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Sorry for all the questions. Rashes make me panicky.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ask as many as you need. Stop the amoxicillin and the cream, start the cetirizine tonight, and I'll see you in two weeks.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: Amoxicillin since Monday for sinusitis three times daily is supported; status 'currently_used' is wrong because doctor stopped it today.
bad.text: amoxicillin (frequency=three times a day, duration=since Monday, indication=sinusitis, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Amoxicillin dose discrepancy includes the nurse/script stating 500 mg three times daily, while the patient reports the bottle says 250 mg three times daily; the patient said she checked before leaving.
Rash morphology was described by the patient as red bumps, with some lesions joining up.
Patient reported the rash is not migratory: 'Mine doesn't move, it just stays and itches.'
Patient said she 'can't think' in the context of the rash/itch.
Patient denied fever on the day of review ('I don't feel hot today').
Doctor noted no pus and no spreading hot edge on examination when explaining why this was not cellulitis/infected.
Doctor stated that blood tests or a scan would not answer this and are not planned.
Doctor planned to record both sides of the allergy history specifically: husband remembers a childhood penicillin rash and the patient denies it.
